title: Responses must fit the barrier

blocks.heading: Responses must fit the barrier
blocks.text: Possible urban-growth responses include self-help housing, site-and-services schemes, rural development and planned new towns. These responses address different mechanisms and require resources, participation and continuing services; judge them by delivered access and functioning services. An urgent water-service failure needs a different first response from a shortage of job opportunities or serviced residential land. Identify affected residents, feasibility and an implementer. Compare improvements to existing areas with relocation: a distant site may solve a land constraint while making jobs less accessible. The stated criterion should guide the choice.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Self-help schemes
blocks.text: Self-help housing involves residents contributing labour, decisions or resources to improve or build shelter, usually with suitable supporting arrangements. It may use local capability and staged improvements but can exclude people lacking time, physical capacity, finance or secure access. An invented community has willing builders and appropriate materials but needs technical support and a safe service connection. Supported self-help may fit those capabilities. Requiring households already working long hours to build unaided is a different proposition. Participation should be feasible and service responsibilities clear; self-help does not mean abandoning residents to provide everything.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Site and services schemes
blocks.text: A site-and-services scheme provides planned plots with essential supporting services or access arrangements, with housing often developed in stages. It can address a serviced-land shortage, but affordability, location, secure usable access and continued service maintenance determine who benefits. A plot without a practical work connection can increase travel costs. A plot price above residents’ means leaves the access problem unresolved. Compare real household capabilities and the site’s services rather than treating a grid of plots as completed housing provision. This is a conceptual scheme, not a statement of current local allocation law.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Rural development projects
blocks.text: Rural development can improve livelihoods, services and opportunities in rural areas. It can expand genuine choices and reduce some pressures to migrate, but does not automatically reverse urbanisation or replace urban service provision. Repairing a farm-market connection may improve the viability of rural work where products and buyers exist. People can still prefer or need to move for other reasons. Judge the programme by rural well-being and opportunity, not by treating movement itself as a failure. Topic 5.1 develops the productive strategies in more depth.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: New towns
blocks.text: New towns are planned settlements intended to provide an organised location for housing, work and services. They can distribute activity and provide planned infrastructure, but require substantial coordination, finance and real links between homes, jobs and services. In a fictional proposal, serviced housing is available far from employment without affordable transport. Relocation may shift rather than solve the access problem. A town with credible work opportunities and maintained services has a stronger basis. Compare timing and costs with improving existing settlements; a planned name does not establish a complete community.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Compare an urgent and a longer response
blocks.text: An invented existing settlement has an urgent water-access gap. A funded extension can connect it to nearby usable supply; a new town would take several years and its job connections are unresolved. The extension better fits the immediate access criterion, while long-term housing planning remains relevant. In a different case, a well-connected serviced site may solve a land shortage more directly. A recommendation names the implementer, the practical action and why it fits the evidence. Local authorities, service providers and residents can have different responsibilities; do not imply residents alone must finance a network.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect causes and responses
blocks.text: Match the time horizon and access problem to a feasible response. Rural Development in Topic 5.1 complements urban provision rather than replacing it.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
